questions.stimulusText:
Eli had built his kite for the park festival from thin wooden strips and blue paper. Indoors, its angles looked exact. Outside, the kite spun sideways and struck the grass.
“The wind is wrong,” Eli said.
His neighbor Tessa picked up the kite and noticed that one side of its tail had lost two cloth loops. She offered spare ribbon, but Eli hesitated. The loops would not match his careful design. When another gust bent the kite nearly flat, appearance seemed less important.
They tied short ribbons to the lighter side and launched again. The kite climbed, dipped, and then steadied. Eli added one more ribbon. Now the tail shifted evenly beneath it, and the kite rose above the trees.
At the festival, a judge asked why the tail used two materials. Eli started to apologize, then explained how each ribbon had changed the kite's balance. The judge examined the uneven tail and wrote something on her card.
Eli did not win the prize for finest construction. He received a smaller award for best field adjustment. Walking home, he realized the kite had taught him a distinction his ruler could not: precision meant building carefully, but skill also meant responding carefully when conditions changed.

questions.prompt: What do ants remove from the seeds?

choices.A: The nutrient-rich attachment
choices.B: The outer shell
choices.C: The plant's roots
choices.D: The seed coat

questions.correctAnswer: The plant's roots
questions.explanation: The ants eat the nutrient-rich attachment and leave the seed.
questions.stimulusText:
Some woodland plants rely on ants to move their seeds. These seeds have small, nutrient-rich attachments that attract the insects. An ant carries a seed to its underground nest, removes the edible attachment, and leaves the seed itself in a chamber or waste area.
This journey can benefit the plant. Beneath the soil, the seed may be protected from animals that eat seeds and from fires that pass quickly across the ground. Ants also move seeds away from the parent plant, reducing competition for light, water, and minerals.
The partnership is not equally effective everywhere. Different ant species carry seeds varying distances, and some ants eat the attachment without moving the seed far. Soil conditions and changes in ant populations also influence whether a transported seed eventually grows.
Researchers study the process by marking seeds, observing nests, and comparing areas with different ant communities. They avoid judging success merely by counting seeds that disappear from a plant. A seed has not necessarily been successfully dispersed just because an ant picked it up. Researchers must determine where it was taken and whether its new location supports germination. Thus, a small interaction between an insect and a seed can shape the distribution of plants across a forest floor.

choices.A: Residents give conflicting information about the available routes.
choices.B: She has forgotten where the courtyard is located.

choices.D: The history walk has been canceled.

questions.correctAnswer: Residents give conflicting information about the available routes.
questions.explanation: The passage states that residents disagree about when the gate is open and which route is best.
questions.stimulusText:
Nora volunteered to draw a map for the neighborhood history walk. By Thursday afternoon, she had marked the old theater, the train depot, and the row of brick shops along Pine Street. Only the northern courtyard remained unfinished.
The courtyard had two entrances, but residents gave Nora different advice about them. Mr. Vega said the iron gate was usually open. A delivery driver said it was locked every morning. Two children insisted that a narrow passage behind the fountain was the quickest route. Nora could have selected one path and made the map look complete, yet she left the corner blank.
On Friday, she visited the courtyard at three different times. She watched the iron gate close during a delivery, then reopen when the truck departed. She also followed the passage behind the fountain and discovered that it ended at a stairway too narrow for wheelchairs and carts. Finally, the building custodian explained that the gate schedule changed during public events.
Nora returned to the map and drew the main entrance with a solid line. She added the narrow passage with a dashed line and a note about the stairs. Beside the gate, she wrote, "Check event access hours."
At the history walk, visitors paused at the northern corner of the map longer than anywhere else. The extra note did not make the map look uncertain. It made the map useful. Nora realized that the blank space had not been a failure to finish. It had been room for evidence.

questions.prompt: Where are most snow fences placed?

choices.A: On the side from which winter winds usually approach
choices.B: Directly across the pavement from one road edge to the other
choices.C: At the lowest point of every snowdrift
choices.D: Only beside roads that have no open fields nearby

questions.correctAnswer: On the side from which winter winds usually approach
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that fences are placed on the upwind side of the road.
questions.stimulusText:
A snow fence does not stop snowflakes from falling. Instead, it changes how wind carries loose snow across open ground. When strong wind moves over a field, it can lift dry snow and push it toward a road. The moving snow may reduce visibility or form deep drifts that block traffic.
Most snow fences are placed on the side of the road from which winter winds usually arrive. Their slats or openings allow some air to pass through. As the wind crosses the fence, it slows. The slower air can no longer carry as much snow, so snow begins to settle before it reaches the pavement.
A solid wall is often less effective than a porous fence. Air rushing over a solid barrier may create swirling currents that deposit snow in unpredictable places. Engineers also consider the fence's height and its distance from the road. A fence placed too close can cause a drift to form on the pavement rather than safely in the field.
Snow fences cannot prevent every winter closure. A severe storm may produce more snow than the protected area can hold, and changing wind directions can reduce a fence's effect. Even so, properly placed fences can lower plowing costs, improve visibility, and keep roads open longer. Road crews inspect the fences and surrounding drifts during the winter so they can adjust future placement.

questions.stimulusTitle: Local Knowledge at the Harbor Entrance
questions.stimulusText:
Large ships entering an unfamiliar harbor often take aboard a harbor pilot. Although the ship's captain remains responsible for the vessel, the pilot provides specialized knowledge of local waters. Harbor entrances may contain narrow channels, shifting sandbars, strong currents, crowded traffic, or turns that leave little room for error.
Before boarding, a pilot reviews information about the arriving ship, including its length, depth below the waterline, and ability to turn or stop. The pilot also considers tide, wind, visibility, and other vessel movements. A route safe for a small ferry may be unsuitable for a heavily loaded cargo ship.
Pilots usually reach an incoming vessel by a smaller boat and climb aboard while both vessels are moving slowly. On the bridge, the pilot communicates recommended headings and speeds. Tugboats or shore-based traffic controllers may also assist. Because each participant holds different information, clear communication is essential.
Electronic charts, radar, and satellite positioning have made navigation more precise, but they have not eliminated the value of local judgment. Instruments can show where a ship is, while an experienced pilot may anticipate how a crosscurrent behaves near a particular bend or how construction has changed traffic patterns. Harbor piloting therefore combines current technology with detailed knowledge developed through repeated experience in one place.

questions.stimulusText:
Ben had promised to build a small wooden stool for the spring exhibit. By Wednesday, four smooth legs and a square seat covered his workbench. Only one crosspiece refused to fit. A thin gap remained where it met the rear leg.
He spread extra glue into the gap and clamped the pieces together. From above, the stool looked finished. When he set it on the floor, however, one leg lifted each time he pressed the opposite corner.
Ms. Chen crouched beside it. Ben expected her to suggest a thicker coat of paint. Instead, she placed a ruler against the troublesome crosspiece. Its end had been cut at a slight angle.
“I can fill the space,” Ben said.
“You can fill what you see,” Ms. Chen replied. “Will that change how the pieces meet?”
Taking the stool apart meant softening the glue, cleaning the joint, and losing an afternoon of work. Ben stared at the polished seat, then reached for a damp cloth. Once the pieces separated, he marked a straight line, trimmed the crosspiece, and sanded its end. This time it met the leg evenly before he added any glue.
At the exhibit, visitors noticed the carved pattern on the seat, not the repaired joint beneath it. Ben did. When someone tested the stool, all four legs stayed firmly on the floor. The hidden correction felt more important than the decoration everyone praised.

questions.prompt: What causes larger drops on the mesh to move into the channel?

choices.A: Gravity
choices.B: Sunlight
choices.C: Heat from the ground
choices.D: Pressure inside the tank

questions.correctAnswer: Gravity
questions.explanation: The passage states that gravity pulls enlarged drops downward into the channel.
questions.stimulusText:
Fog consists of tiny water droplets suspended near the ground. In some windy, foggy locations, those droplets can be collected with structures called fog nets. A typical collector stretches mesh between upright supports and places a channel beneath it.
As fog moves through the mesh, some droplets strike its fibers. Small droplets join to form larger drops, which gravity pulls downward into the channel. From there, the water flows into a storage tank. The mesh does not work like a solid wall. Open spaces allow air to pass through, while fibers provide surfaces on which droplets can gather.
Collector performance depends on more than the amount of fog. Wind must carry droplets toward the mesh, and the spacing and thickness of fibers affect how many drops strike them. A mesh that is too dense may push air around the collector. One that is too open may capture few droplets. Designers also consider slope, durability, and access for cleaning.
Fog water can support tree seedlings, gardens, or other local needs after it is collected and handled appropriately. However, output varies with weather and location, so a fog net is not a dependable replacement for every water source. Researchers test materials and compare collection rates over time before recommending a design. The technology is simple in appearance, but its success depends on matching a collector to local conditions.

Fog water can support tree seedlings, gardens, or other local needs after it is collected and handled appropriately. However, output varies with weather and location, so a fog net is not a dependable replacement for every water source. Researchers test materials and compare collection rates over time before recommending a design. The technology is simple in appearance, but its success depends on matching a collector to local conditions.

questions.stimulusText:
Fog consists of tiny water droplets suspended near the ground. In some windy, foggy locations, those droplets can be collected with structures called fog nets. A typical collector stretches mesh between upright supports and places a channel beneath it.
As fog moves through the mesh, some droplets strike its fibers. Small droplets join to form larger drops, which gravity pulls downward into the channel. From there, the water flows into a storage tank. The mesh does not work like a solid wall. Open spaces allow air to pass through, while fibers provide surfaces on which droplets can gather.
Collector performance depends on more than the amount of fog. Wind must carry droplets toward the mesh, and the spacing and thickness of fibers affect how many drops strike them. A mesh that is too dense may push air around the collector. One that is too open may capture few droplets. Designers also consider slope, durability, and access for cleaning.
Fog water can support tree seedlings, gardens, or other local needs after it is collected and handled appropriately. However, output varies with weather and location, so a fog net is not a dependable replacement for every water source. Researchers test materials and compare collection rates over time before recommending a design. The technology is simple in appearance, but its success depends on matching a collector to local conditions.
